title: De Gaulle's rise, fall and rise again
gist: A short notebook of three cultural recommendations: praise for Antonin Baudry's De Gaulle biopic Resistance, a nod to Andrew Pettegree's history of bookselling as companion to Philip Hensher's novel history, and admiration for a Proms performance of Beethoven's Seventh Symphony.

insights.claim: The first instalment of Antonin Baudry's De Gaulle biopic, Resistance, is built on Julian Jackson's biography A Certain Idea of France and features Simon Russell Beale as Churchill, delivering a thrilling, historically convincing and at times moving account of the early war years.
insights.speaker: Paul Lay
insights.so_what: A recommendation signal for a historically grounded war film with prestige-cast appeal.
insights.quote: this is a thrilling, historically convincing and, at times, rather moving affair
insights.locator: De Gaulle: Resistance, the first part

insights.claim: The film weaves De Gaulle's struggle to convince Churchill of his worth with the radicalisation of Admiral Darlan's assassin Fernand Bonnier de La Chapelle, though it makes little of the killer's monarchism.
insights.speaker: Paul Lay
insights.so_what: Notes a narrative choice, the underplayed monarchist motive, that critics and history-minded viewers may weigh.
insights.locator: Weaving De Gaulle's struggle to convince Churchill

insights.claim: Andrew Pettegree's The Bookshop: A History of Bookselling is presented as the perfect companion to Philip Hensher's A History of the Novel in Britain, with the argument that democracy was born through the commercial industry of bookselling and publishing.
insights.speaker: Paul Lay
insights.so_what: Frames the book trade's commercial 'dirty' work as foundational to democratic culture, a corrective to purist views of literary value.
insights.quote: it is by such industry that our democracy was born
insights.locator: There are those who would no more

insights.claim: The author rates Beethoven's Seventh Symphony as his greatest, echoing Wagner's description of it as the 'apotheosis of the dance', praising the Swedish Chamber Orchestra under clarinettist-conductor Martin Frost at the BBC Proms.
insights.speaker: Paul Lay
insights.so_what: A performance recommendation and a critical judgement ranking the Seventh above Beethoven's other symphonies.
insights.quote: Wagner described Beethoven's Seventh Symphony – his greatest, in my opinion – as the 'apotheosis of the dance'
